title: Speak good or stay silent
hook: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, speak good or be silent, honor the neighbor and the guest (Nawawi 15, Abu Hurayrah)
carry: say good or stay silent, and honor neighbors
tomorrow: a man asks for advice and gets two words. why say them again?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard hadith read with care, and its heart: blood is sacred. A life is not a thing to take. Today the forty turn to something people break far more often: a sentence.

Saturday, seven in the morning, and the line at a coffee counter runs out the door. The man at the front has waited four minutes and wants everyone to hear about it. Behind the counter, the answer is already loaded, and it is sharp, and it would feel great. Across the street, the owner of a brand-new bakery is unlocking her door for the first time, glancing over. A customer waiting. A neighbor watching. One sentence could go either way, and there's a hadith built for exactly this second.
screen: `A LINE OUT THE DOOR.` → `THE ANSWER IS LOADED.` → `A NEIGHBOR WATCHING.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Al-Nawawi's fifteenth hadith, in paraphrase. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say good or stay silent. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. Look at how it's built: the same opening three times. Faith in the Last Day, the biggest thing there is, gets checked in three small places. The mouth. The fence. The front door. And the first line offers two doors, not one. Not 'only say nice things.' Not 'never speak.' Good, or silent. If what's coming is good, say it. If it isn't, the second door is always open, and it costs nothing. Silence here isn't sulking or the cold shoulder; it's simply not adding the bad sentence. Then the neighbor. The hadith doesn't ask what the neighbor believes. One report has the Prophet's companion Abdullah ibn Umar, when a sheep was slaughtered at his house, asking twice: have you sent some to our Jewish neighbor? Then he quoted the Prophet: Jibril kept urging me about the neighbor until I thought he'd make him an heir. Something to tell a friend tonight: the sheep, the question asked twice, and the neighbor of another faith at the center of it. Good, or silent.
screen: `THE SAME OPENING, THREE TIMES.` · `THE MOUTH, THE FENCE, THE DOOR.` · `TWO DOORS: GOOD, OR SILENT.` · `HAVE YOU SENT SOME NEXT DOOR?` · then, large: `GOOD, OR SILENT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the day's first complaint come up: a slow line, a late reply, the noise next door. Don't say it, not even in your head. Hold it like a cup you've decided not to pour, and let it cool for the length of the sit.
Good: khayr in Arabic, the first door in today's hadith. If it's good, say it. If it isn't, the second door, silence, never locks.
Your line: say good or stay silent, and honor neighbors. The neighbor on the other side of the wall counts too. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1443 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY · 15 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN ASKS FOR ADVICE AND GETS TWO WORDS. WHY SAY THEM AGAIN?`

howItsDone: This hadith is memorized as part of al-Nawawi's Forty and quoted at home, in class and in Friday sermons; in some homes it shows up as a plate sent next door and tea for whoever drops by.

fork.setup: your group chat is roasting a classmate who isn't in it. you have a genuinely funny line ready. by today's hadith, what's the move?
options: post something good about her, or post nothing.
post it with 'jk'; a joke isn't really speech.
leave every chat that ever has gossip in it.
fork.reveal: good, or silent: two doors. a joke at someone's expense isn't the first one, and the second door is always open.

original.note: Arabic: good, goodness. In the hadith, 'let him say khayr, or stay silent.'

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule about being polite.
what it means: faith in the Last Day, checked in three places: what you say, how you treat the neighbor, how you treat the guest.
what a scholar hears: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 and Sahih Muslim 47 with their triple opening, and Ibn Umar's question about his Jewish neighbor in Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1943.
guess: khayr: what's worth saying out loud
khayr: polite words, true or not

chat.says: running dad's counter alone 😤 a guy just yelled at me, and the new bakery lady saw. clap back?
options: say something good to him, or nothing. then go welcome the bakery lady.
clap back politely; honesty is good, so tell him exactly how rude he was.
say nothing to anyone today; silence is always the holier, safer choice.
chat.meaning: The hadith gives two doors, good or silent, and pairs your tongue with honoring the neighbor. The bakery next door counts.

tie.story: Ibn Umar, with a sheep slaughtered at home, asked twice whether some had been sent to his Jewish neighbor.
tie.friend: Amira can take the second door with the yelling customer, then walk over and welcome the new neighbor.
tie.you: Which neighbor could you honor this week?

khayr.meaning: good, goodness; the first door in the hadith

al-Nawawi.meaning: the scholar from Syria who gathered the Forty

hadith.meaning: a report of what the Prophet said or did

Abdullah ibn Umar.meaning: a companion of the Prophet, son of Umar

Jibril.meaning: the angel Gabriel, who brought revelation

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 15; Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, Sahih Muslim 47 (Abu Hurayrah)
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1943; Sunan Abu Dawud 5152 (Ibn Umar and the Jewish neighbor; Jibril kept urging about the neighbor)
